new_statements.quote: 12. Words of two syllables are accented on the first syllable: as, Rō'ma, fi'dēs, tan'gō. Words of more than two syllables are accented on the Penult if that is long (as, amī'cus, monē'tur, contin'git); otherwise on the Antepenult (as, do'minus, a'lăcris, dissociā'bilis). a. When an enclitic is joined to a word, the accent falls on the syllable next before the enclitic, whether long or short: as, dĕă'que, ămārē've, tĭbī'ne, ită'que (and ... so), as distinguished from i'tăque (therefore). [footnote:] The Penult is the last syllable but one; the Antepenult, the last but two.

Minor transcription differences only: the page prints breves on the pre-enclitic vowels, 'dĕă'que, ămārĕ've, tĭbĭ'ne, ită'que' (reader wrote ămārē've, tĭbī'ne with macrons), and 'do'mĭnus', 'dissociā'bĭlis' (reader dropped the breves); the sentence 'So (according to some) ex'inde, ec'quandō, etc.' is silently elided before the footnote. new_statements.rule_in_words: Classical penultimate law: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; in longer words stress falls on the penult if it is heavy (long), otherwise on the antepenult. Stress never goes further left than the antepenult. With an enclitic (-que, -ve, -ne) the accent moves to the syllable immediately before the enclitic regardless of its weight.
new_statements.exceptions: §12 Exceptions (p. 7): (1) apparent compounds of faciō keep the accent of the simple verb (benefa'cit, calefa'cit); (2) genitive and vocative of 2nd-declension nouns in -ius and genitive of -ium keep the accent of the nominative (Cornē'lī, Vergi'lī, ingē'nī); (3) words that lost a final vowel keep the accent of the full form (illī'c for illī'ce, prodū'c for prodūce, satī'n for satīsne). §15.2 Note (p. 8): vowel weakening in compounds 'is commonly ascribed to an accentuation on the first syllable, which seems to have been the rule in Latin before the rule given above (see § 12) became established. The original Indo-European accent, however, was not limited by either of these principles; it was probably a musical accent so-called, consisting in a change of pitch'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both grammars describe classical Latin (Allen & Greenough p. 8: the language of the classical period, B.C. 80 - A.D. 14). Allen & Greenough §15.2 Note adds that pre-classical Latin probably had initial-syllable accent and that the Proto-Indo-European accent was a pitch accent; neither is a statement about classical Latin word stress. The PuRe copy for work 0 is the 1903 edition, not the 1979 reprint the catalog cites.

new_statements.quote: 6. 1. Words of two syllables are accented upon the first; as, tégit, mōrem. 2. Words of more than two syllables are accented upon the penult (next to the last) if that is a long syllable, otherwise upon the antepenult (second from the last); as, amāvī, amántis, míserum. 3. When the enclitics -que, -ne, -ve, -ce, -met, -dum are appended to words, if the syllable preceding the enclitic is long (either originally or as a result of adding the enclitic) it is accented; as, miseróque, hominísque. But if the syllable still remains short after the enclitic has been added, it is not accented unless the word originally took the accent on the antepenult. Thus, pórtaque; but míseráque.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule field is empty; Bennett gives the same weight-sensitive penult/antepenult placement as Allen & Greenough and adds an explicit syllable-weight definition and a more differentiated enclitic rule (weight of the pre-enclitic syllable matters, unlike Allen & Greenough's 'whether long or short').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Same penultimate law: disyllables first syllable; longer words penult if the penult is a long (heavy) syllable, else antepenult. Syllable weight is defined in §5 B (p. 5): long if it has a long vowel, a diphthong, or a short vowel before x, z or two consonants (muta cum liquida makes a 'common' syllable, short in prose). Enclitics: the syllable before the enclitic is accented only if it is long; if it stays short the word keeps its original accent (pórtaque) or, per Bennett's example, carries both (míseráque).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned as such; the example míseráque (p. 5) marks two accents on one enclitic-bearing word.
new_statements.exceptions: §6.4 (p. 6): loss of final -e of -ne/-ce does not affect the accent (tantón, istíc, illāc, vidén for vidésne); §6.5: utríque and plēráque accent the penult by analogy with utérque, utrúmque, plērúmque although -que is not a true enclitic there. Footnote p. 5: 'To avoid confusion, the quantity of syllables is not indicated by any sign.'

tone_statements.quote: While stress- and pitch-based accent systems are not necessarily mutually exclusive, one is nevertheless relatively more essential than the other for a given language. Based on recent typological studies provided by phoneticians and phonologists, it is most likely that the Italic accent had a dominant stress nature in the period when vowel reduction (and deletion as its extreme form) occurred – a conclusion that partly favours the views of German School. [...] languages with pitch accent may have accentual contrasts within a single syllable [...]. There seems to be no such phenomenon observable for Latin or Italic in general.

tone_statements.citation: Deroy, Louis. 1981. Les apparentes contradictions de l'accentuation latine. L'Antiquité Classique 50(1-2): 222–234.
tone_statements.quote: En particulier, la caractère « musical » de l'accent latin classique a été trop souvent conçu comme identique à celui de l'ancien accent grec, alors qu'il ne lui est que superficiellement comparable.
tone_statements.translation: In particular, the 'musical' character of the classical Latin accent has too often been conceived as identical to that of the ancient Greek accent, whereas it is only superficially comparable to it.
tone_statements.locator: p. 222 (first page; Persée document page text)

tone_statements.citation: Sturtevant, Edgar H. 1940. The Pronunciation of Greek and Latin. 2nd ed. Philadelphia: Linguistic Society of America.
tone_statements.quote: 214. The evidence compels us to conclude that in the period of the classical and postclassical literature the Latin accent involved both stress and high pitch upon the same syllables. For stress we have abundant evidence also for both the preclassical and the latest periods; but we learn directly of the Latin pitch only for the period from about 100 B.c. to about 300 a.p. It is probable, however, that it existed both earlier and later. In fact, it is not unlikely that the considerable element of pitch in the modern Italian accent is a direct inheritance from Latin.
tone_statements.locator: p. 189, ch. VII 'The Latin Accent', sec. 214; cf. sec. 206 p. 177 and sec. 212 pp. 187-188
tone_statements.summary: One word accent, placed by rule on penult or antepenult, carried both stress and high pitch on the same syllable in classical Latin; pitch is part of that accent, not a separate lexical tone contrast.

tone_statements.citation: Laurand, L. 1938. L'accent grec et latin: remarques et bibliographie choisie. Revue de philologie, de littérature et d'histoire anciennes 64 (3e sér. 12): 133–148.
tone_statements.quote: Sans prendre parti ni discuter la question, je signalerai brièvement quelques faits qui se dégagent de ces discussions infinies ou quelques erreurs définitivement réfutées. ... En étudiant les arguments apportés de part et d'autre pour l'accent purement musical et pour l'intensité pure, on a grand'peine à en trouver qui soient absolument sans réplique. Aussi n'est-il pas étonnant que des savants de plus en plus nombreux proposent d'admettre à la fois hauteur et intensité. Ainsi les partis adverses se réconcilieraient.
tone_statements.translation: Without taking sides or arguing the question, I shall briefly point out a few facts that emerge from these endless discussions, or a few errors that have been definitively refuted. ... Studying the arguments brought on either side for a purely musical accent and for pure intensity, one is hard put to find any that are absolutely unanswerable. So it is not surprising that more and more scholars propose to admit both pitch and intensity at once. Thus the opposing parties would be reconciled.
tone_statements.locator: p. 135, remarks after the taxonomy of opinions, and p. 138, close of the remarks on the arguments
tone_statements.summary: Surveys the dispute over whether the Latin accent was musical (pitch), intensive (stress) or both, and expressly declines to decide; notes growing support for pitch and intensity together.

tone_statements.citation: Kent, Roland G. 1932. The Sounds of Latin: A Descriptive and Historical Phonology. Language 8(3), Language Monograph No. 12: 11–216. Baltimore: Linguistic Society of America.
tone_statements.quote: German and English scholars generally hold that the Latin accent was one of stress, like that of English, a view borne out by the phenomena of the language. But French scholars follow the Roman grammarians, who describe the Latin accent as characterized by higher musical pitch, like that of ancient Greek. The real status was probably as follows: At first the Latin accent was characterized by energy or stress ... From that time on, Latin was spoken with a pitch accent by the highly educated class, while the general populace retained the stress accent.
tone_statements.locator: p. 66, sec. 66 'The Latin Accent', I (second paragraph)
tone_statements.summary: Holds the Latin accent was a stress accent placed by the penultimate law, not tone; a Greek-style pitch accent was only an educated-class fashion c. 150 B.C.-300 A.D., after which stress prevailed.

tone_statements.citation: Abbott, Frank Frost. 1907. The Accent in Vulgar and Formal Latin. Classical Philology 2(4): 444–460.
tone_statements.quote: The solution may be found, I think, in the theory that in the sermo plebeius the accent was primarily a stress from the earliest period to the latest, but that in the literary language during the classical period the stress-element became secondary to the pitch. To this conclusion both the statements of the grammarians and the facts of the language point. ... they give rules for the incidence of the circumflex and acute accents which find no counterpart in Greek.
tone_statements.locator: p. 451 and p. 459, running argument, no section headings
tone_statements.summary: Argues literary Classical Latin had a pitch (musical) accent, with the grammarians' acute and circumflex (incidence fixed by quantity), while popular Latin kept a stress accent; literary stress returns by the 5th-6th c.

tone.summary: One word accent, placed by rule on penult or antepenult, carried both stress and high pitch on the same syllable in classical Latin; pitch is part of that accent, not a separate lexical tone contrast.

tone.translation: Without taking sides or arguing the question, I shall briefly point out a few facts that emerge from these endless discussions, or a few errors that have been definitively refuted. ... Studying the arguments brought on either side for a purely musical accent and for pure intensity, one is hard put to find any that are absolutely unanswerable. So it is not surprising that more and more scholars propose to admit both pitch and intensity at once. Thus the opposing parties would be reconciled.
tone.summary: Surveys the dispute over whether the Latin accent was musical (pitch), intensive (stress) or both, and expressly declines to decide; notes growing support for pitch and intensity together.

sources.citation: Kent, Roland G. 1932. The Sounds of Latin: A Descriptive and Historical Phonology. Language 8(3), Language Monograph No. 12: 11–216. Baltimore: Linguistic Society of America.
sources.quote: German and English scholars generally hold that the Latin accent was one of stress, like that of English, a view borne out by the phenomena of the language. But French scholars follow the Roman grammarians, who describe the Latin accent as characterized by higher musical pitch, like that of ancient Greek. The real status was probably as follows: At first the Latin accent was characterized by energy or stress ... From that time on, Latin was spoken with a pitch accent by the highly educated class, while the general populace retained the stress accent.
sources.locator: p. 66, sec. 66 'The Latin Accent', I (second paragraph)
sources.note: Holds the Latin accent was a stress accent placed by the penultimate law, not tone; a Greek-style pitch accent was only an educated-class fashion c. 150 B.C.-300 A.D., after which stress prevailed.

sources.citation: Abbott, Frank Frost. 1907. The Accent in Vulgar and Formal Latin. Classical Philology 2(4): 444–460.
sources.quote: The solution may be found, I think, in the theory that in the sermo plebeius the accent was primarily a stress from the earliest period to the latest, but that in the literary language during the classical period the stress-element became secondary to the pitch. To this conclusion both the statements of the grammarians and the facts of the language point. ... they give rules for the incidence of the circumflex and acute accents which find no counterpart in Greek.
sources.locator: p. 451 and p. 459, running argument, no section headings
sources.note: Argues literary Classical Latin had a pitch (musical) accent, with the grammarians' acute and circumflex (incidence fixed by quantity), while popular Latin kept a stress accent; literary stress returns by the 5th-6th c.
